chunks:
Economic opportunity in a county rarely detaches from the health of its local balance sheets. Before small businesses borrow to rebuild after a hurricane or municipal treasurers price local school bonds, deposits have to sit inside insured regional intermediaries. Pulling every single row from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) 2024 Summary of Deposits—all **76,727 U.S. bank branches**—and rolling them deterministically onto five-digit `county_fips` keys exposes breathtaking spatial inequality in where American savings pool.

The FDIC conducts its branch-level deposit census every June 30 across every insured commercial bank and thrift nationwide. As the FDIC Summary of Deposits reporting guide states:

> "The Summary of Deposits is the annual survey of branch office deposits as of June 30 for all FDIC-insured institutions, including insured U.S. branches of foreign banks."

Because FDIC records publish without API keys via paginated JSON endpoints, our open [databases](/explore/databases) pipeline pulls every branch record (`STCNTYBR`, charter `CERT`, and deposits `DEPSUMBR` in thousands of dollars), maps 76,672 county-matched branches onto 3,195 U.S. counties totaling **$17,395,742.37 million ($17.40 trillion) in deposits**, and isolates **38 banking-desert counties** holding zero FDIC-insured branches.

## Reading the Contrast Between Charlotte, Wake, and Rural Mississippi

Comparing deposit footprints across North Carolina and Mississippi shows how national clearing hubs distort state totals while leaving peripheral counties thin: 1. **North Carolina ($693.32 Billion Across 1,986 Branches & 2 Banking Deserts):** North Carolina anchors one of America's largest commercial banking centers.

**Mecklenburg County** alone holds **$432,277.42 million ($432.28B)** across 240 branches representing 36 unique FDIC charters—followed by **Wake County ($90,333.80M across 240 branches and 35 banks)** and **New Hanover County ($18,423.42M across 52 branches)**. Together, Mecklenburg and Wake account for three-quarters of North Carolina's entire statewide deposit base, even as 2 smaller NC counties register zero physical FDIC bank branches. 2. **Mississippi ($77.82 Billion Across 1,055 Branches & 0 Banking Deserts):** Mississippi maintains remarkably broad county branch distribution—zero of its 82 counties lack an FDIC branch—yet operates on roughly one-ninth the total deposit capital of North Carolina.

**Hinds County** holds **$8,244.05M** across 62 branches (even amid -$133.79M IRS AGI outflow), **Madison County** holds **$5,258.47M** across 55 branches, and **Rankin County** carries **$4,411.13M** across 52 branches.

## Addressing the Headquarters Booking Caveat

Financial regulators and [austrian economics](/explore/austrian-economics) analysts always issue one vital warning when interpreting Summary of Deposits rankings: major money-center banks frequently book billions in wholesale, sweep, and treasury deposits onto flagship downtown headquarters branches—such as Charlotte (Mecklenburg), Wilmington (Delaware), or Manhattan (New York County, $1.62T)—even when depositors live nationwide. Raw county deposit sums therefore exaggerate retail household wealth in clearing cities.

Even after adjusting for headquarters booking, tracking unique charter competition (`fdic_unique_banks_2024`) alongside [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights) `banking_desert_flag` rows delivers clean ground truth: knowing whether rural residents face a local two-bank oligopoly or zero physical branches explains real credit friction directly in [civic data benchmarks](/explore/civic-data-benchmarks).

## Using County Deposit Data for Community Resilience

Run a single SQL filter ordering your home state by `fdic_unique_banks_2024 ASC` and place it right next to `irs_net_agi_millions` and `banking_desert_flag` inside a local browser notebook. Tracking both raw deposit concentration and institution charter diversity tells a much richer story than branch headcounts alone: when three separate branches belong to a single acquirer following a regional merger, local business lending authority often narrows sharply even if the physical brick storefronts temporarily stay open.

By inspecting annual June 30 FDIC Summary of Deposits snapshots alongside IRS tax migration and federal emergency declarations, community development financial institutions, rural credit unions, small-business coalitions, and county treasurers gain an empirical early-warning radar. Together, these open public tables highlight exactly which agricultural or industrial corridors remain creditworthy, competitive, and well-served—and which fragile counties risk losing their last remaining loan officer before the next regional downturn arrives.

---
**Sources:** [FDIC 2024 Summary of Deposits Open Data API](https://banks.data.fdic.gov/api/sod?filters=YEAR%3A2024&format=json) · [FDIC SOD Survey Methodology](https://www.fdic.gov/regulations/resources/call/sod.html) · [CFPB Rural & Underserved Counties Guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/compliance-resources/mortgage-resources/rural-and-underserved-counties-list/)

chunks:
Capital and labor vote first with Form 1040 filing addresses, long before school bond referendums or property revaluations show up in county budgets. Across the 3,219 U.S. counties linked inside Marigold's 2022–2023 IRS Statistics of Income migration release, household income reallocation runs into billions of dollars per metro corridor each year—rewriting local hospital financing, infrastructure solvency, and [civic data benchmarks](/explore/civic-data-benchmarks) denominators simultaneously.

Official federal tax statistics track annual interstate and intercounty capital shifts directly from primary tax-return filings. As the IRS Statistics of Income migration overview notes:

> "The annual county-to-county migration tables provide insight into the economic impact of residential mobility by pairing moving return counts with aggregate adjusted gross income leaving and entering each jurisdiction."

Measured purely by net Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) across the 2022–2023 cycle, national capital concentration mirrors classic [austrian economics](/explore/austrian-economics) incentives: households and retirees departing high-tax, high-cost dense metros while flocking toward Sunbelt coastal and suburban jurisdictions. Top national net AGI inflow counties include **Palm Beach, FL (+$3,017.15M despite -1,358 net returns, reflecting steep per-return wealth of newcomers)**, **Collier, FL (+$2,245.72M)**, **Maricopa, AZ (+$1,370.09M)**, **Lee, FL (+$1,256.09M)**, and **Denton, TX (+$1,219.25M)**—offset against massive net AGI outflows from **Cook, IL (-$4,464.45M; -42,264 individuals)**, **Los Angeles, CA (-$4,383.48M; -86,523 individuals)**, **New York, NY (-$3,164.37M)**, **Santa Clara, CA (-$3,131.57M)**, and **King, WA (-$2,195.24M)**.

## Mississippi vs. North Carolina Inside the 2022-2023 AGI Ledger

Zooming onto our 182 benchmark counties inside [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights) exposes an equally sharp regional divergence: 1. **North Carolina's +$3,898.23 Million Expansion:** Across all 100 counties, North Carolina absorbed **+39,207 net tax returns** and **+$3,898.23M ($3.90B) in net AGI**. Inflow leaders spanned **Brunswick County (+3,474 returns; +$502.07M AGI)**, **Wake County (+3,843 returns; +$363.56M AGI)**, **Buncombe County (+1,011 returns; +$238.07M AGI)**, **New Hanover County (+1,277 returns; +$226.23M AGI)**, and **Union County (+1,342 returns; +$201.81M AGI)**—even as central banking hub Mecklenburg saw slight net AGI outflow (-$16.04M) alongside +3,632 net incoming returns as suburban buyers spread outward. 2.

**Mississippi's -$68.36 Million Net Drawdown:** Across 82 counties, Mississippi posted **-3,094 net returns** and **-$68.36M net AGI**. Suburban **Madison (+$44.51M; +157 returns)** and Gulf Coast **Hancock (+$33.66M)** and **Jackson (+$32.04M)** gained filers, but **Hinds County (-1,415 returns; -$133.79M AGI)**, **Rankin (-$37.43M)**, and **Lauderdale (-$19.03M)** pulled the statewide ledger negative.

## Counterargument: Why Single-Year AGI Flows Overstate Structural Decline

Municipal finance analysts caution against treating a single IRS tax-filing window—especially 2022–2023's unusual post-pandemic remote-work settling and capital-gains volatility—as a permanent straight-line forecast. One billionaire domicile shift in Florida or a single tech-vesting windfall can swing county `irs_net_agi_millions` by hundreds of millions without reflecting median household wage health.

Pairing IRS flows with multi-year Census domestic migration (`net_domestic_mig_2020_2024`) and [public health benchmarks](/explore/public-health-benchmarks) separates transient capital-gains spikes from persistent tax-base erosion: when a county loses tax returns, young families, and acute hospital beds together for four consecutive years, municipal bond coverage tightens fast.

## Inspecting Local Fiscal Solvency Yourself

Download the Zstd Parquet file directly into Marigold's browser SQL workbench—or stream state slices via `/api/civic-lake?format=arrow`—and sort your state's counties by `irs_net_agi_millions` alongside `net_domestic_mig_2020_2024` and local bank deposit shares. Instead of waiting two years for delayed property-tax roll reassessments or five-year Census ACS summaries, school finance officers, county commissioners, and rural hospital trustees can trace taxable household income shifting across county borders almost in real time.

Look closely at counties experiencing compounding negative trajectories: persistent negative Form 1040 return balances paired with high adult disability burden and fragile single-hospital coverage demand targeted regional consolidation and disciplined capital budgeting long before bond covenants break. Conversely, rapid-growth coastal and Piedmont counties posting hundreds of millions in annual AGI inflows require proactive school construction, precinct expansion, and water infrastructure planning immediately to avoid administrative bottlenecks during peak population arrival.

---
**Sources:** [IRS 2022-2023 County Inflow Data](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/countyinflow2223.csv) · [IRS 2022-2023 County Outflow Data](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/countyoutflow2223.csv) · [Census 2020-2024 Population Estimates](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2024/counties/totals/co-est2024-alldata.csv)

documents.source_label: [web-omni] Pipes editorial · Reading IRS SOI County-to-County Tax Migration Without Confusing Household Churn for Fraud
chunks: Every two years, activists and local commentators compare state voter registration totals against five-year American Community Survey (ACS) population tables, spot counties sitting above 98% or 100%, and declare proof of phantom voter lists. Yet five-year ACS averages pool sixty consecutive months of household interviews, meaning fast-growing retirement corridors always appear statistically under-populated compared with real-time DMV registrations. Pulling annual Internal Revenue Service Statistics of Income (SOI) county migration files gives [civic data benchmarks](/explore/civic-data-benchmarks) an independent, tax-return-verified thermometer for annual population movement.

The IRS constructs these public migration tables directly by comparing anonymized filing addresses across consecutive tax seasons without ever releasing taxpayer identities. As the IRS Statistics of Income documentation explains:

> "The SOI Migration data are based on year-to-year address changes reported on individual income tax returns filed with the IRS, presenting both inflows and outflows of tax returns, personal exemptions, and adjusted gross income at state and county levels."

When parsed using proper `latin-1` decoding across all 3,096 inflow and 3,111 outflow county FIPS units—normalizing `96,000` U.S.-plus-foreign summary rows and negative `-1` suppression sentinels—analysts gain three crisp economic variables inside [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights): `irs_net_returns` (`n1`), `irs_net_individuals` (`n2`), and `irs_net_agi_thousands` (`agi`).

## Testing Active Registration Outliers Against Annual Tax Filings

Joining IRS 2022–2023 return migration onto Census 2020–2024 demographic series and 2024 EAVS registration benchmarks clarifies opposing demographic trajectories immediately: 1. **Genuine In-Migration Growth:** Coastal **Brunswick County, North Carolina (37019)** registers 99.61% EAVS active voters per CVAP (and 106.08% in 2026 state totals). Cross-checking IRS 2022–2023 filings confirms 7,974 incoming tax returns versus 4,500 outgoing—**+3,474 net returns, +6,320 tax-filing individuals, and +$502.07 million in net Adjusted Gross Income** in a single year alongside +33,821 four-year Census net domestic migration. New taxpayers are physically moving in faster than five-year ACS windows update. 2.

**Stagnant Roll Shrinkage:** Conversely, **Hinds County, Mississippi (28049)** records a 102.28% EAVS active-to-CVAP ratio while IRS data shows **4,226 inflow returns against 5,641 outflow returns (-1,415 net returns, -2,660 individuals, and -$133.79 million net AGI)** matching -17,670 Census domestic out-migration. The high ratio reflects unremoved former residents in [election integrity](/explore/election-integrity) confirmation queues rather than surging arrivals.

## Weighing What IRS Migration Misses

Responsible analysts in [austrian economics](/explore/austrian-economics) and regional demography still recognize clear limits in tax-filing denominators. IRS SOI files under-count low-income households below Form 1040 filing thresholds, miss university dormitory populations claimed as dependents in other counties, and apply small-flow suppression when fewer than 10–20 returns move between a specific pair of counties.

Because summary `96,000` totals aggregate domestic and international moves together while still respecting taxpayer privacy, they remain far cleaner for county-level net balance audits than unverified social-media anecdotes. Paired alongside Census annual death counts and EAVS `A10a` confirmation notices, three independent public series cross-validate one another cleanly.

## Auditing Your Home County in Thirty Seconds

The next time a viral infographic flags a county sitting above 100% voter registration, pull its five-digit `county_fips` row from the 2022–2023 IRS SOI migration lake before jumping to conclusions about clerical impropriety or illegal enrollment. Compare four companion columns side by side inside a local SQL workbench: `irs_net_returns`, `irs_net_agi_millions`, `net_domestic_mig_2020_2024`, and EAVS confirmation-notice completions.

When IRS filings show strongly positive `irs_net_returns` and `irs_net_agi_millions` alongside positive Census net domestic migration—as documented in Brunswick County and Wake County, North Carolina—an elevated registration ratio typically signals rapid suburban or retirement expansion outpacing five-year ACS survey lag. Conversely, when steep negative return and AGI outflows persist alongside shrinking population, election boards have an objective civic cue to prioritize National Voter Registration Act Section 8 confirmation mailings and inactive-to-removed queue hygiene. Grounded federal data literacy turns partisan heat into measurable administrative light.

---
**Sources:** [IRS SOI Tax Stats Migration Portal](https://www.irs.gov/statistics/soi-tax-stats-migration-data) · [IRS 2022-2023 County Inflow CSV](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/countyinflow2223.csv) · [U.S. Census Population Estimates Methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest.html)

chunks:
Most civic analytics dashboards collapse under their own serialization weight long before a researcher finishes a second SQL filter: shipping ten-megabyte raw CSV or JSON blobs across serverless boundaries burns cold-start RAM and turns browser tabs sluggish. By adopting open-source columnar primitives already built into Python, Node, and browser WebAssembly—**Zstd-compressed Apache Parquet**, **Apache Arrow IPC streams**, and **unsupervised Expectation-Maximization (EM) Fellegi-Sunter linkage**—small investigative teams gain true warehouse performance at essentially zero hosting cost.

The speed difference comes from organizing memory by column rather than row so analytical engines skip untouched fields entirely. As the Apache Arrow specification states:

> "The Arrow columnar format defines a language-independent memory layout for flat and nested data organized for efficient analytic operations on modern CPU and SIMD hardware without serialization overhead."

When applied directly inside [databases](/explore/databases) pipelines for Marigold's five national federal datasets, compiling CSV releases into Zstd Parquet slashes wire payloads dramatically while preserving exact leading zeros on five-digit `county_fips` keys: the 487.3 KB U.S. County Atlas shrinks to **192.8 KB**, the 321.6 KB OpenFEMA continuity file drops to **81.9 KB**, and the 346.8 KB CDC PLACES plus HHS hospitals dataset compresses cleanly to **112.1 KB**.

## Three Server FOSS Primitives Built for High-Integrity Audits

Combining server compaction with [local-first](/explore/local-first) WebAssembly execution gives citizen auditors three reusable superpowers:

1. **Parquet Shards + HTTP Range Execution:** Compiling 50,000+ raw federal filings (76,727 FDIC branches, 19,551 OpenFEMA declarations, 7,621 HHS hospital rows) on the server emits tiny Zstd Parquet shards loaded straight into browser `DuckDB-Wasm` via `read_parquet(...)`. Every user executes full SQL joins locally without waiting on remote database pools. 2. **Zero-Copy Arrow IPC Endpoints (`/api/civic-lake?format=arrow`):** When a client wants a state-filtered slice (`?state=NC` or `?state=MS`), the server serializes typed `Float64Array` and UTF-8 Arrow buffers directly into `application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` bytes and streams them straight into DuckDB-Wasm via `insertArrowFromIPCStream`, avoiding JSON parsing tax completely. 3.

**Unsupervised Fellegi-Sunter EM Entity Resolution:** Inspired by UK Ministry of Justice's open-source Splink engine, server-side EM optimization estimates field match weights $\log_2(m_k / u_k)$ directly from unlabeled agreement matrices over public non-PII institutions (hospital `CCN` ↔ charter `CERT` ↔ county FIPS) without manual rule tuning, complementing client-side [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights) deduplication and [public health benchmarks](/explore/public-health-benchmarks).

## Confronting the Over-Engineering Counterargument

Full-stack skeptics reasonably argue that three-thousand-row county files parse quickly as plain CSV, making Parquet and Arrow seem unnecessary until datasets exceed millions of rows. While true for tiny slices, building the binary pipeline cleanly on five county tables establishes the exact zero-copy rails needed when scaling to **84,000 U.S. Census tracts** or **10M+ public CMS provider rows** tomorrow—with zero architectural rewrite.

## Running Your Own Sovereign Data Refinery

Inspect `/api/civic-lake` headers in your terminal or click any starter card on `/data-stories` to watch this split compute architecture run live in a standard browser tab: notice how public **Zstd Parquet** shards (`PAR1`) and typed **Apache Arrow IPC** streams mount directly into isolated `DuckDB-Wasm` WebAssembly workers in milliseconds, while sensitive user-supplied voter rolls or municipal spreadsheets remain strictly inside local encrypted memory and never cross a network wire.

Equally important for long-term civic reproducibility, every server-compiled Parquet and CSV lake file ships alongside explicit SHA-256 checksums in `manifest.json`, zero-PII automated validation tests in continuous integration, Empirical Bayes shrinkage baselines for tiny rural counties, and deterministic Fellegi-Sunter EM entity-resolution parameters. Open-source columnar formats and client-side WebAssembly engines eliminate expensive cloud warehouse lock-in, banish third-party tracker bloat, and turn massive public transparency datasets into fast, mathematically auditable software anyone with an ordinary laptop can inspect, query, and verify independently from start to finish.

---
**Sources:** [Apache Arrow Columnar Format Specification](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html) · [Apache Parquet Zstd Documentation](https://parquet.apache.org/docs/) · [Fellegi & Sunter Record Linkage Theory (JASA 1969)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1969.10501049)
